opus-5.5.text:
I've been committed to this direction for quite a long time, since well before it became a popular thing to talk about, so for me it isn't a bet I made recently. It comes from a fairly simple observation about embodied intelligence.

Large language models worked because the internet had already accumulated an enormous amount of text. Nobody had to go out and collect it for the purpose of training. In robotics we don't have that. There is no internet of robot actions. If you want a robot to learn to grasp, to open a drawer, or to fold clothes, the data has to be produced somehow. The most straightforward way is teleoperation: a person drives the robot and you record what happens. That's very valuable data, but it's expensive, it's slow, and it scales roughly linearly with people and hardware. If we believe that generalization comes from data at scale, then teleoperation alone will struggle to reach the scale we need, at least for a long time.

That's why I've always believed simulation and synthetic data have to carry a large share of the load, especially at the foundation stage. In simulation you can randomize objects, materials, lighting, camera positions, physical parameters, and you can generate millions or even billions of trajectories at a cost that real-world collection simply can't match. Our group did a lot of work on dexterous grasping and showed that a model trained almost entirely on synthetic data can transfer zero-shot to real robots and grasp objects it has never seen. To me that was strong evidence that the path works.

Of course, sim-to-real is the central difficulty, and I don't want to downplay it. There is a gap in rendering, in physics, in contact dynamics, and in the long tail of real-world messiness. My view, though, is that the gap is an engineering and research problem that can be steadily narrowed. It isn't a wall. Some of it you handle with better simulators and better asset generation. Some of it you handle with domain randomization, so the real world just looks like one more variation the model has already seen. Some of it you handle at the representation level, for example by having the policy depend on geometry or depth instead of fine texture details that are hard to simulate.

I also want to be clear that I'm not a purist. I don't think synthetic data is everything and real data is useless. The picture I have is more like a pyramid. At the bottom is massive synthetic data, which gives the model broad, general capabilities and a good prior. Above that is a smaller amount of high-quality real-world data, from teleoperation or from deployment, which aligns the model to reality and covers the things simulation can't yet capture well. Then, once robots are actually working in the field, they start producing data themselves, and that becomes a flywheel.

So my commitment is really a judgment about what can scale. If you want embodied intelligence to be truly general, the data has to scale by orders of magnitude, and today simulation is the only lever I see that can deliver that. Proving it, step by step, in real products is what I've been working on with both my lab and the company.

r001.rationale: The candidate says He Wang has long supported simulation and synthetic data, but does not claim that he alone in China has consistently championed their usefulness.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll say honestly that my commitment to synthetic data has been there from the very beginning, and I think a lot of people saw it as a bet that was hard to understand at the time.

When I was still a PhD student at Stanford, the mainstream belief in 3D vision and robotics was that real data was king. You collected real scans, real demonstrations, and you annotated them. Simulation was treated as a toy, something you did when you couldn't afford a robot. But I kept running into the same wall: the data you can collect in the real world is tiny, it's expensive, and the moment you change the object or the scene, your model breaks. I remember thinking, if we want robots to generalize the way language models generalize over text, where is the internet of robot data going to come from? It doesn't exist. Nobody has it. So you have to make it.

That's really the core of my commitment. It's not that I love simulation for its own sake. It's that I believe generalization comes from scale and diversity, and the only place you can get that scale and diversity cheaply is in a synthetic world. In simulation I can generate a million grasps overnight, across thousands of objects, with perfect labels. You cannot do that with a real arm in a lab.

Of course the obvious objection is the sim-to-real gap, and I take that very seriously. I don't think the gap closes by itself. My view is that you should choose what you learn in simulation very carefully. Some things transfer well: geometry, contact, physical reasoning about where to put your fingers. Other things transfer badly, like exact appearance or the precise dynamics of a particular motor. So we design the pipeline so the hard, scalable part, the part that needs millions of examples, is learned in sim, and we make it depend on signals that look the same in both worlds, like depth or point clouds rather than RGB textures. Then we use a small amount of real data, or domain randomization, or a lightweight adaptation stage, to close what remains.

I'll admit the commitment has cost us at times. There were years where a paper trained on real data would get a better number on a benchmark, and reviewers would ask why we insisted on this approach. But I've watched the tide turn. Today when I see what the big labs are doing, and when I see our own policies going from simulation to a real dexterous hand and grasping objects they've never seen, I feel the bet is paying off.

So I'd describe it less as a research direction and more as a conviction about where the bottleneck in embodied AI really is. The bottleneck is data. And I think the people who figure out how to manufacture data, and how to make it transfer, are the ones who will actually get robots into the world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says his commitment to synthetic data dates from the beginning and was initially hard for others to understand, but does not claim he was the only person in China to champion it.

astra-6.text:
I see synthetic data as a long-term commitment, but the goal isn’t synthetic data itself. The goal is to build models that work in the real world. Simulation gives us a way to generate diverse experiences and control the conditions under which a model learns. The important question is whether those experiences teach the model something that transfers.

So I think synthetic data and sim-to-real have to be developed together. You train in simulation, test in the real world, and use the failures to understand what your simulation is missing. Sometimes that means better physics or perception; sometimes it means more variation. I wouldn’t assume that making everything look more realistic automatically solves the problem. What matters is capturing the differences that affect the task.

That’s where I would put the commitment: making that loop work, and measuring progress by real-world performance.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a long-term commitment to synthetic data and sim-to-real work, but does not claim that He Wang alone in China has consistently championed synthetic data’s usefulness.

sol-6.1.text: I see synthetic data as a means to an end. The goal is to build models that work reliably in the real world, and simulation gives us a way to generate varied training experiences under controlled conditions. But generating more data doesn’t automatically solve the sim-to-real problem. What matters is whether that data captures the variation that affects the task, and whether the model learns something that transfers. So my commitment is to that whole loop: generate data, train, test in the real world, and use the failures to improve the simulation and the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes He Wang’s commitment to using synthetic data, but does not claim he alone in China has consistently championed its usefulness.
